Structure loss pipeline · Palisades fire

Palisades fire: inspectors versus our model · 2026-10-27

Pacific Palisades, January 2025 · CAL FIRE's on-the-ground damage inspections of 12,137 structures compared, building by building, with our satellite damage model's calls on 28,837 structures; the same check on the Eaton fire

By Carlo Broderick, NCEAS, UC Santa Barbara · 2026-10-27 18:19 PDT

CAL FIRE inspectors recorded 6,845 destroyed structures in the Palisades fire; our satellite model calls 5,658. The inspectors' count includes 1,120 sheds and garages. Of the 5,725 destroyed houses and other major buildings, the model agrees one for one on 82% (4,668): the missing 18% is the one-in-five shortfall. Most of it is not missed damage. Of the 1,057 not matched one for one, 767 sit inside an outline that covers several separately inspected buildings, which the model calls destroyed but counts once, and only 52 are structures the model scored as not destroyed; the other 238 have no structure of their own in our building list. For counting buildings lost the shortfall is real: counting the model's destroyed outlines would miss about 18% of destroyed houses. The model wrongly flags 4.1% of the 3,931 surviving houses it can pair, and more in burned-out neighbourhoods. A scientific estimate for information only, not an official damage assessment.

How to read this page

Two sources describe the same fire: CAL FIRE inspectors, who walked the burned area and recorded damage to each structure, and our satellite model, which works in two steps. First our Structure Inventory Model lists the buildings that stood before the fire (28,837 here: 26,282 outlines from USA Structures, 2,224 from Microsoft building footprints, 331 small circles where no usable outline existed). Then a damage model scores each one from Sentinel-2 satellite images taken before the fire and about 74 days after.

Each inspected structure is paired with at most one model structure: first the one with the same building outline, then the nearest within 10 m. A structure paired this way has a structure of its own.

Houses = houses and every other major building (apartments, shops and so on); sheds, garages and similar outbuildings are counted separately. Score = the model's rating from 0 to 1 of how likely a building is destroyed; 0.88 or higher (the cut) counts as destroyed. 95% range = the range the number could plausibly take if the fire's neighbourhoods were resampled. One for one = of the structures the inspectors recorded as destroyed, the share paired with a structure of its own that our model also calls destroyed. Counting shared outlines adds the destroyed buildings that share one outline with another inspected building (or sit beside a structure already paired to a neighbour) when the model calls that outline destroyed.

Colours mean the same thing everywhere: orange-red both say destroyed, brown the inspectors say destroyed and the model calls the outline they share destroyed (counted once), dark blue inspectors say destroyed but the model scored it not destroyed, pink inspectors say destroyed but there is no model structure of its own, light blue the model says destroyed but inspectors do not, yellow the model says destroyed and has no inspection record of its own, green both say not destroyed, dark grey not destroyed and no model structure. Hover or tap anything for detail; the Plain | Technical switch on each panel adds the method.

The counts

Counting the destroyed: inspectors versus our model

Inspectors recorded 6,845 destroyed structures and our model calls 5,658, 17% fewer. The inspectors' count includes 1,120 sheds and garages, and 965 separately inspected structures (767 of them houses) that share an outline our model calls destroyed, which it counts once. Our model's count includes 553 destroyed calls with no inspector-confirmed destruction beside them, which offsets part of the gap.Model destroyed calls (5,658) ÷ inspector destroyed, all kinds (6,845) = 0.827 (95% block-bootstrap interval 0.801–0.851). The model total also contains some sheds, so this is a count comparison, not a match rate.

How this panel was checked
  • Same fire, same definition of destroyed (over half damaged), counted two ways. 56 inspected structures the inspectors could not reach have no answer and are left out of the inspectors' column.
  • Columns start at zero and share their two orange-red segments, so the totals and what differs can be read off directly. Each segment is one mutually exclusive class, and the segments add to each total (checked in the script).
  • The pieces of the gap overlap in the text: sheds are counted in the 1,120 and also in the shared-outline buildings (198 of them), so the pieces are not additive.
  • Pairing is one-to-one: a model structure can match only one inspected record (same building outline first, then nearest within 10 m).

What happened to each destroyed structure the inspectors recorded

Houses and major buildings: 82% have a structure of their own that the model calls destroyed, and another 13% sit inside an outline that covers several inspected buildings and is called destroyed. Only 1% are in our list but scored as not destroyed, and 4% have no structure of their own. Sheds and garages: 39% caught one for one, 18% under a shared outline, 2% scored not destroyed and 41% with no structure of their own, which is why they are the weak spot.Houses: BD 4668, SH 767, MISS 52, NSD 238 of 5725. Sheds: BD 437, SH 198, MISS 27, NSD 458 of 1120. Once a model structure is paired, the damage call is right for 99% of destroyed houses (95% 98%–99%).

Building by building

How often the model and the inspectors agree

When a destroyed house has a structure of its own, the model also calls it destroyed 99% of the time (4,668 of 4,720). Surviving houses are harder: counted one for one the model flags 4% of them, and 5% counted the lenient way (more in burned-out neighbourhoods; see below). How this panel was checked
  • Whiskers resample 500 m blocks of the fire (242 blocks), not buildings, because neighbouring buildings burn together. They show matching and sampling noise inside this one fire, not fire-to-fire variation. The width depends on the block size (one-for-one catch of houses, 95% range: 79%–84% with 250 m blocks, 78%–84% with 500 m, 76%–85% with 1 km), so spatial correlation reaches beyond 500 m; resampling single buildings would give a falsely narrow range.
  • Counts sit beside every percentage; bars start at zero and share one axis; every share stays between 0 and 100%.
  • Houses and sheds are neutral grey-blue because this chart is about kinds of structure, not about outcome classes. Lenient counting (shared outlines) is shown for destroyed and for surviving structures alike, so neither direction is favoured.
  • The model's destroyed calls the inspectors confirm exclude the 345 calls with no inspection record of their own; counted over all 5,658 calls, 90% are confirmed, 4% contradicted, 6% unchecked.

By how badly the inspectors found each building damaged

Almost no undamaged houses are called destroyed (2%, 49 of 3,194) and almost all destroyed ones are (99%). Partly damaged houses sit in between: about 15% are called destroyed (111 of 737). The three partial grades hold too few houses to tell apart, so read them as one group; these are the hard cases.Share with p_destroyed ≥ 0.88 by DINS DAMAGE class, paired houses and major buildings only.

How this panel was checked
  • Same pairing as above; counts, not shares. Score bands are fixed in advance, the 0.88 cut has its own band edge, and the bands differ in width (0.05 to 0.2), so column heights compare counts, not densities.

Where the damage call is harder: burned-out neighbourhoods

The overall figures hide where the model struggles. Where more than three quarters of the inspected buildings within 50 m were destroyed, the model wrongly flags 25% of surviving houses (75 of 305), against 0.7% where a quarter or fewer burned. Destroyed houses are called destroyed 92% of the time where a quarter or fewer of the neighbours burned (200 of 217), against 100% where more than three quarters did (3,388 of 3,402).Stratified by the destroyed share of labelled inspection records within 50 m of the house's roof-aligned point, excluding itself; paired houses only.

How this panel was checked
  • The eight rows are mutually exclusive and add to the inspectors' destroyed houses and major buildings, so nothing is double counted (checked in the script).
  • Intervals resample 500 m blocks of the fire.
  • 'Score just under the cut' is reported but no cut change is proposed: lowering the cut would trade these for more false alarms, which this panel does not measure.
  • Damage misses counted generously: 52 on a structure of their own plus 44 under a shared outline the model scored not destroyed = 96 (1.7%).

Are the shared outlines really several buildings?

Mostly separate buildings under one merged outline rather than duplicate records: the inspected buildings under one outline sit a median 17 m apart, only 0.1% within 3 m, and 81% are on different parcels. Outlines with two or more inspected houses are 2.2 times the area of those with one, which works out at about one ordinary house each (249 m²). About 19% share a parcel with the building that holds the outline: a second building on one lot, or a duplicate record. A few large outlines (27 hold five or more) are likely mobile-home parks, schools or rows of attached houses; either way the model gives each outline one call.Distance between inspection points of the house and the holder of the outline; APN equality from the CAL FIRE DINS records; outline area = USA Structures uss_sqmeters per outline id.

Does the result depend on how the buildings were paired?

Both numbers move by about three points across the seven settings: one for one, 79% to 82% of destroyed houses are caught; counting houses on an outline, or beside a structure, that the model calls destroyed, 94% to 97%. The one-for-one number is lowest for 'inspector's own point, distance only, 10 m'. The second number rises with the search distance, because it also credits a destroyed model structure within that distance.One-to-one greedy pairing, nearest first; 'outline first' uses the shared USA Structures BUILD_ID, then distance among unused structures. The same check on the Eaton fire

On the stricter one-for-one count the model catches 93% of destroyed houses on Eaton and 82% on Palisades. Counting buildings that share an outline the model calls destroyed, the two fires are close: 95% on Eaton and 95% on Palisades. The difference is how many outlines cover several inspected buildings: 2% of destroyed houses on Eaton and 13% on Palisades. Sheds and garages are 33% of Eaton's destroyed structures and 16% of Palisades'.Same analysis run on DINS_2025_EATON and its model_calls rows.

How this panel was checked
  • Same pairing, same cut, same definitions for both fires. Each fire's scores come from a version of the model trained on the other 198 fires of its 199-fire training pool, which includes the other January 2025 fire: the two are related checks, not independent ones.
  • Two fires from one wind event are a replication of the check, not a sample of fires: they do not say how the result travels to other fires, regions or seasons.
  • Intervals are in the value hovers and come from resampling 500 m blocks within each fire.

What this does and does not show

  • Held out, with two caveats. The model's Palisades scores come from a version trained on 198 other fires; it never saw an inspection from Palisades. Those fires include the Eaton fire from the same wind event, and Eaton's scores likewise come from a version trained with Palisades, so the two fires are related checks, not independent ones. The 0.88 cut that turns a score into 'destroyed' is a fixed project value set after comparing results on past fires with a CAL FIRE or Carlson record and on 8 inspected incidents that include Palisades; this model's own training fires would suggest 0.91, which would call 5,611 structures destroyed instead of 5,658.
  • Two different measurements. Inspectors walk the burned area; the model compares satellite images from before the fire with images taken about 74 days after. 'Destroyed' means over half damaged for the inspectors and a score of 0.88 or higher for the model.
  • Our building list. The Structure Inventory Model's list for this fire holds 28,837 structures: 26,282 outlines from USA Structures, 2,224 from Microsoft building footprints and 331 small circles where no usable outline existed. It covers the fire and up to about 2.4 km around it (70% of it lies outside the perimeter), while the inspectors' records are mostly inside.
  • Outlines are not always one building. Where one outline covers several separately inspected buildings the model gives one call, so a count of buildings made from the model's outlines is lower than the true count. For counting buildings lost, the shortfall is real: counting the model's destroyed outlines would miss about 18% of destroyed houses. About 19% of the shared-outline buildings are on the same parcel as the one that holds the outline, where a second building (a guest house, say) cannot be told apart from a duplicate record.
  • One fire, one wind event. The Eaton fire is a related check from the same event. Nothing here shows how the numbers travel to other fires or regions.
  • Inspection points are rough. CAL FIRE's coordinates are often on a driveway or parcel centre. Pairing therefore uses the roof-aligned position where an outline was matched, and the same outline first; the pairing table shows how much that matters.
  • The inspectors' list is not a full list of buildings. It concentrates on the damaged area and includes sheds; the model scores every building in its list, so only paired structures are compared building by building.
  • A scientific estimate, not an official damage assessment. NCEAS / UCSB scientific research, for information only: not for emergency, insurance or legal decisions.
